entities.name: John VII of Hoya
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
John VII of Hoya (died 1535), a German count and formidable military commander, played a pivotal role in the Scandinavian conflicts of the early 16th century, most notably the Count's Feud (Grevens Fejde) from 1534 to 1536. Born into the influential House of Hoya, a noble family with significant holdings in northern Germany, he was a brother to Eric of Hoya, who served as Prince-Bishop of Münster and Osnabrück. John VII emerged as a key military leader for the Hanseatic city of Lübeck and its Swedish allies, aiming to restore Christian II to the Danish throne and challenge the rising power of the Danish monarchy under Christian III.

His military career saw him command considerable forces, leading campaigns across Denmark and Sweden. In 1534, John VII was instrumental in the initial successes of the Lübeck-Swedish coalition, capturing strategic strongholds and engaging royalist forces. He was dispatched by Lübeck's burgomaster, Jürgen Wullenwever, to support the Swedish regent Gustav I Vasa and later to lead forces on Funen. His strategic acumen and battlefield presence were crucial during the early stages of the Count's Feud, as he sought to consolidate control over key Danish islands and resist the forces loyal to Christian III.

John VII's ambitions and military prowess met their end on June 11, 1535, at the Battle of Øxnebjerg on the island of Funen. Leading the combined forces of Lübeck and the rebellious Danish nobility, he was decisively defeated by Christian III's royal army, commanded by Johan Rantzau. John VII himself perished in the battle, a critical turning point that significantly weakened the Lübeck-Swedish alliance and paved the way for Christian III's eventual victory and the establishment of the Reformation in Denmark. His death marked a major setback for the Hanseatic League's attempts to reassert its influence in Scandinavia, contributing to Lübeck's gradual decline as a regional power.
